Stephanie Slattery, the algebra teacher for eighth grade, had to stop herself from weeping in the border checkpoint. She'd lasted five years, most of them at Hawthorne, and one grade level above blew it every year. Now this one had tackled the fat problems. The gun was still blazing across the heavens; her boss had run to his car and robbed her of those last hours; so she came home early to the lounging dog and the wet snow and the empty house. She clapped off the wet snow in the drive and walked upstairs looking for a place to weep where someone wouldn't find her. Rain had leaked through the roof in the bathroom, and she called a roofer the contractor had recommended.

With school out, she'd had a chance to clean house for Thanksgiving, finally throwing out papers that didn't matter anymore. On Friday afternoon she'd found herself bagging things that had been like extra credit problems, like guardianship, whose answers didn't matter because they'd always been checked by someone else. She was grief-stricken and grieving alone. Maybe no one was left to mourn her ninth-graders anyway. Maybe they had made the mental downgrade to drop-outs.
Allis Amberson had just been promoted to night manager at Chesterfield's Gas and Go on 102, on the south edge of town, off the four-lane. It had been a cool-seeming day for December, with a sky that made people stand around counting white pellets flickering over the bright asphalt in laps. She did reconnaissance of the lot from the two-story break room to see who might need to be sent home early because of the canyons rising from slick morning asphalt. Most of her staff were twenty-somethings, none of them with kids, and the only one who couldn't drive was the old guy they called Dad. So they watched the rain lift and fall all morning. One young woman who didn't know the relationship of these things to bus schedules asked what homecoming game Allis was going to, and Allis knew why her mother had told her when she was eighteen to only date the sons of weathermen. Allis adjusted the antennas on the weather radio on the front counter: national plus local plus All Hazards. Everyone turned on their headlamps.

He'd wear holes in the bottoms of his boots, he knew, but he threw up a wall around Jake's house, mounded into the porch and up the windows.

Jake's office at the junior college was only a couple blocks from home. In his headlights on the way to work Gus wondered how long Jake had slept outside before he came home. He wondered if Jake would make it through the night with the snow falling so thick.

You take something awful and you shackle it, he thought, you try to control it. Afternoon turned to dusk, then disappeared like it did on those days when the land was hidden in haze. And it happens. Sometimes more often than you like. The line gives and you're left with something new.

Gus turned the blade off and got out. "You don't got one," he said to the sky, "do you?" He came back inside and turned on the news.

It started with a flake. The flake's name was Hollis Boss and she lived with her parents in Mason City, Iowa. Mason City was built on a flood plain, with levees that protected it more or less and dikes to keep the Mud Creek water out. Meteorology was a perennial campus subject at George Wythe University in Mockingbird, fifteen miles away, so Hollis, whose family worried about dullness, had chosen an English major and switched to history in her second year.

Hollis spent a lot of time with her head down studying and walking in the city with big earmuff headphones over her ears. Even that minimal exposure was enough to convince her that life moved awfully quickly for Mason City folk. Hastings and Waverly, and even Nauvoo, were only a half-hour away; there were people who left Mason City and never came back, sometimes because of abuse or crime or scandal, sometimes just to do something different, and sometimes no one knew for sure. Whole families. When it rained they changed neighborhoods, when it snowed they left the state, wheeling themselves off on planes and Greyhound buses wondering if they'd ever see Mason City again. And it snowed a lot. Maybe more snowes than no-snowes.

The Boss family wasn't from Mason City originally but had come to the same place together as a fresh start group following the cybersecurity boom of the early 2010s. When Hollis, an ephemerologist today, was almost five years old, her parents started baking pies and cakes on the weekends while Hollis crawled up at the foot of the bed to watch them turn Le Mans and Reading and the Birdhouse. "I don't care if they blow us off or they come," her mother said to Hollis and her father one Saturday night. "Just to get it out there. I emailed about pie orders at my old job but nobody's responding. Maybe we should put a box in front of the library, anyway."

Anger constricted his chest. How much were they going to let this drift get in their heads? Why didn't they just clear the snow and get on with life?

The snow came down in wisps for another hour. Gus waited until the flakes settled a little and bundled up in his snowsuit and hat, and trudged out to the truck to unhitch the blade. He found it hard to be mad at the storm anymore—three inches wasn't that bad for a town shielded from the full brunt of winter.

But a car exploded past him and hit the bank of snow across the street with enough force to pole-vault up and over it and down the slope to the curb. From outside Hawthorne Elementary, a crowd of people shouted and whistled. Gus watched them swarming to the overturned car, flailing through the snow and shoving and shouting, until at last someone wrapped the window down and freed a lady trapped inside.

Gus left the truck in the drive and went indoors. He set a couple of chairs over the warm register on the first of the three bedrooms of the small house. There was a plate with leftovers from supper on the formica table in the kitchen. He ran water from the faucet, and the plate simmered in the steam. Down the hall his father snored loudly in his bed. The furnace would come on before it got too cold in the night, but won't there ever be a night like all the other ones?

Friday, December 15

The storm was over; the snow wouldn't fall again, so Gus didn't plow.

Friday Gus went to the mechanics shop before work; he could afford a payment that day, and it was a good week for tips at the distribution center. He bought groceries at the stoplight store, then a hotdog at the last hotdog stand on his route home. He took another shower and changed into a shirt that he'd kept clean for nine days so that he'd have a fresh one to wear to work on Saturday.

The streets in the business district were slush-filled trenches. He worked carefully to avoid splashing pedestrians as he went about his deliveries. He took lunch on his box truck, eating quickly. Between 2:00 and 3:00 he gathered all of his collections and loaded them into the back. When the snow melted he would be able to count them quickly and deposit the money into the office safe.

It was a long day. He didn't get out of the last dropoff until 5:45, and one of his customers had left a pint of gin for him in the cab. He had a couple of drinks while driving back across the city to deliver the three commercial trash cans, and he felt safe driving on slightly frozen side streets in the dark.

At the address, 714 E. Boliner, a thick-curtained Victorian townhouse, Gus pulled the truck sideways, partly blocking the sidewalk. The back of the house on Boliner was on a hill, so the driveway was perpendicular to the road at this point. Gus clicked on the lights inside the cab and opened the doors to dump out the trash cans. The oldest can made too much noise, and he flinched even as he emptied it. He stopped to listen.

No noise except mice, probably.

The first snow of the season arrived at two or three that afternoon in an occasional flurry. The yard fattened a little — a couple of inches. By the time Den had come outside for dinner, four inches had fallen, block the big windows of the living room, keeping the kitchen light from leaking out.

Joe had always loved to sill through snow on a tall, Snoopy-style sled. He'd tried dragging me a couple of times, but I was so small I was scared. I clung to Nanna and refused to let go. That second winter up here, worn out after a concert, she brought me outside to watch the snow. Joe came racing across the yard, and at the last moment slid past us, a trail of delicate vapor pouring off his coat, the sled smoking through the snow, a lion bar in his fingers.

This afternoon he was building another fort, and I sat at the dining room window to watch. Through the gathered dusk of snow, I could see a black form moving in the early-starred heaven, leaving sails of vapor behind it.

I wanted badly to tell Joe about it. If I had been faster at talking, one of the many tales he had not lived to be taught would not have slipped away into oblivion with him. I had the sinking sense that I was drifting farther adrift from the certainties of his childhood and banked away ingredients and memories still living, preserved into sticks of a far older lumber. Without anyone else to tell stories to, they were crumbling back into soil, becoming useless on both sides of the ground.

In a few more months I would have to move somewhere else, probably next year. There was nothing to do now but sift through the remaining branches for repairable memories and ficus roots for trunnions, trying to make a sail that would take us up there, where the man inside the rocket body was living out his childhood.

Gillian R. Molloy, Author

Gus turned up the radio and rummaged in the truck bed for the heater hose. It had leaked a hole and he'd taped it up with duct tape for the winter, but even so it had frozen anyway. A month of disappointment had made him resolute. He was getting drunk.

Soon the snow stuck, and Gus's truck was covered over like a blanket on a sofa. Pulling it out would be impossible. But it wouldn't last long. The radio sounded weird, farther away, like it was playing in the house. But when he turned it off, it got louder. It was coming out the speakers, and there was more of it. Something about the storm, maybe.

He fumbled around for his headphones and off he went, snowed in with music, liquor, and the bottle warmer on full blast.

Gus wasn't high, but he wasn't drunk, either. It had never been that important to him. He heard a knock on the door, quiet at first, but as he reached the doorframe it got louder, reverberating through the house. He swung the door wide and saw a cloud of snow behind a little girl waving through it. She would have been cute but for her oversized boots, clothes, and a voice springing out of her much older.

"You're going to miss the concert if you don't get moving, Gus."

"I was," Gus said. "Sorry, I dropped my headphones. What's your name?"

"Maggie. I'm taking over for Hannah Stewart. Last minute sub, you know how it is." Her eye caught something in the driveway. "How 'bout it, are you going?"

"Sure." Gus grabbed the bed warmer and handed it to Maggie. "I got plenty more."

"Left it on." He grabbed his coat. "Sorry." They rounded back to the driver's seat. "Forgot my keys. I dropped 'em." Gus opened the door and Maggie hopped out into the snow. The flakes were big and heavy. She walked to the middle of the driveway and stopped. Gus stepped out behind her and closed the door. His driveway was gone, and so was the road in both directions. It wasn't possible. Even the garage roof had disappeared somewhere over his head. He looked left and right, pleading for something familiar. Nothing at all. Where was his subdivision? His driveway? Gus laid his head down on the steering wheel and let the silence press in on him from every direction until he felt like he could hear himself breathe.

Gus had read every comment about the decision, and he'd pretty much made up his mind that despite being the right call, the school district had fucked up big time. It was relieved of all liability when people drive in the snow, and even if the road's bad, people should be allowed to decide for themselves if the concert was important enough to take the risk. People drove drunk every year and if that was okay, why wasn't driving in the snow? His wife said she wasn't getting into that snow again if she could avoid it, and he was totally on board with that. Plus, Gage couldn't dress himself, so it probably was a good thing he wasn't crying in the back seat of his mom's truck because he was on his way to throw snowballs at center field. Gas costs money, and driving around doesn't just hurt the environment—it burns oil. What was more important, a school concert for otherwise spoiled kids, or his kid's future? No way was he showing up.

Gus had a job plowing driveways and most of the other parents had jobs, too, so kids in band or chorus saw school just as much as kids who weren't in band or chorus. Kids whose parents drove trucks or vans to work or worked from home drove to school just the same either way, so what's the danger?

These weren't complicated questions, so he was a little surprised that the school district's decision was as controversial as it had turned out to be.

Maybe it was a question of local versus foreign. If school and its events were within the town limits, then maybe we have to care about them because these are our neighbors, our future, our community. The first annoyance was that wrists and hands of every parent and teacher wore buzzing, flashing ID bracelets. When a child's hands got cold they went into mittens and pockets, so the only logical place was behind the ear. One of them chirped every thirty seconds or so as if getting a text from someone out of range. Gus chewed him out for being so nosey every time he chirped, imitating the bracelet sound exactly.

The kids filed into the crowded, noisy gym, but almost before the song began some parents whispered about the parking lot and grabbed each other by the arm. Anxious, medium-blue waves of whispering and indecision wandered through the bleachers between the slow, creaking hymn. They broke spring water on the thirsty brown grass by the door.

Gus tried not to let his complaining annoy the parents heading outside. He asked if anyone would get him a sandwich from the cafeteria so he didn't have to leave the truck. He said yes, thanks to offers from three different women, and texted the office to let them know, then looked around for his next chore. Snow fell in dull white sheets, half a dozen inches thick now. It fairly drowned the brown sticks peeking up from the graves in the churchyard. The little plow pushed easily through the soft, pliant snow, but the weight of the snow on the blade was a problem. Gus stopped the truck, opened the window, and set the snowplow down in the street in front of the car next to the church. He guessed getting in and out of the truck wouldn't interrupt more than a half hour total of plowing. By the time he left, there were ten cars in the street waiting for him.

Everyone in the parking lot was frantic now. One teenager with a NorthPark baseball cap waited for the blizzard to stop before climbing back in his car, using the sideview mirrors as eyes. As soon as the last flake settled on his window, Gus climbed in the truck again and pushed the rest of the cars back onto the street. They idled around hanging on for a solid fifteen minutes. He had to take a break. They knew it, too.

The car in front of him was still running when Gus got back. It was the same car from before, only there was no one sitting in it.

As he waited for the flakes to merge into a flake-file, a 1972 Plymouth Fury drove slowly past. Gus didn't recognize the driver. Then it stopped in the middle of the street and backed up to his house. Gus climbed out of the truck to see who it was.

Four guys climbed out. They were wearing raincoats, work boots, jeans, and work gloves. The oldest was in his late twenties, and his name was Jimmy. He brought a cooler packed with beer from Jimmy's car, in a back alley behind the house, through the blackened top of a broken fence that Gus hadn't fixed in twenty years.

Gus flashed on the bedroom window, hoping the kids hadn't seen. "Hey, Jimmy. The hell'd you get those beer bottles past Colleen?"

The smell coming from the cooler was like what Gus had made himself when he was Jimmy's age. "They're not bottles, Gus. They're aluminum cans. And they're less likely than bottles to get swallowed by a five-year-old."

Gus entertained Jimmy and his friends his way. He shared his best whiskey, a bottle of 2004 Dewar's single malt that had cost him $12 fifty years before. He'd left it for emergencies. No family, no money, no friends—the whiskey was for the days when he was sure he didn't want to live anymore. When he handed over the bottle, he began to think it was an emergency now.

The crew from the job site was used to drinking in the truck on the way to the next job, and they brought cups and shared and swapped stories as each guy stepped from the back yard with a full one. Gus told a retail story—he'd run a small hardware store in the next town over for thirty years, and he still had favorites. The other guys drank up that whiskey, and then they smoked two packs. Gus could smell it on them all night, and his good whiskey, too. He doubled down on the fragrances to drive his wife out.

It worked, eventually. They were standing and applauding when she pulled up the driveway on her husband Stevie's beach cruiser. Gus wished he had triggered the alarm instead. Maybe he'd have a second chance at the whiskey. "

New snow fell steadily until he reached the edge of town, six miles west of the limits, where the gravel highway became a four-lane state road with inattentive truckers. The highways were plowed and sanded, but there was still no way to stay lined up. In thirty years Gus had never had an accident or a near miss, and he wasn't planning to start. He let off and pulled over.

The truck had heated bucket seats and he had a flask of Raever Tororo, so he settled back and kept listening to the radio, twenty miles per hour over the gravel scrape of the blizzard outside. The system had misread the forecast for this county, and the dome didn't retract. The storm lasted until a week before Christmas, when the county got another thirteen inches and the reservoir froze solid. Gus skipped the Hawthorne concert twice that year.

He cleaned a couple sidewalks, made a quick turn around his own driveway to break up the ruts, and shut off the truck. It was nice to spend twenty minutes doing something, even if it didn't count. He could feel the cold sink into his coat, and he wondered what Mr. Moraniac in south Burley was studying to fire up next. Like Mayor Alfred Goor, fifty to sixty percent of the people Gus knew in town loved Reverend Bean, and about that many hated him. Gus had never said anything about Bean, even though he quietly agreed with most of the nice things everyone said.

Tonight he turned on the news at supper and let Bean bang on about the wickedness of the Democratic Party and Governor Bragg. About me

Eli Scarborough is a fifth-year MFA candidate at the Vermont College of Fine Arts. His short fiction has been published in Room Magazine (Canada), Booth, and Lightspeed. He's been a graduate resident editor at Chicago Quarterly Review and senior editor of the Frost Place Literary Residency in Franconia, New Hampshire. When he isn’t reading or writing he’s probably cooking or painting.

Q. Which authors inspire you the most?
Elmore Leonard. He had an amazing ability to create striking, three-dimensional characters and make every word count. James Baldwin. For the way he says a lot more with the most simple and straightforward sentence structures.
Q. What was the hardest part of writing this book?
The hardest part of writing this book was the November to January period, when the characters stopped cooperating and the plot fell apart almost every week. My characters wanted to take the story in a different direction than I wanted to go.
Q. Why do you write?
I write because stories help us understand experiences we don't have. I don't know what it's like to land on the moon, to lose a parent to addiction, or to make a pilgrimage through Tuscany. Stories help me connect with other people and help me make sense of the world.

The north side of town was hills, and when the snow hit the higher elevations, it clung to the ground. By the time it rolled down toward the main street, it was more than an inch high. He worked through lunch, then through dinner, then well past dark, slogging through deeper and deeper snow at fifteen miles an hour in a truck with a flimsy blade and no hand warmers. It would knock off the truck's temperature gauge if it ever got cold enough.

By 8:30 he'd done six driveways and a church and business lot, and he'd made enough money to pay off the truck, but he felt sick and went home early.

Armando and Chava were waiting for him with hot cocoa. He drank some and changed his clothes. "You didn't miss anything," Armando said.

"It didn't start until eight-thirty," Armando said.

He'd been rotating snow images in his mind for hours, thinking that by the time he'd plowed anything significant, any beauty the snow might have had would be mashed flat beneath the weight of the storm. It hadn't mattered either way, but there was a sense of relief seeing the plowed street now, and the gutter spilling crystalline water at the curbside, and his own reflection on the glass as he unbuckled his seat belt and leaned over to give Armando a hug.

He had been ready for his first storm for two years now. He had become obsessed with the weather with the same singular focus that had consumed him in preparing for an accident or a fire at his job as an inspector. His ex-girlfriend had called him "prepared" at first. Later, she called him other things too.

There was no longer time for anything else. He didn't talk at work because he was thinking about plowing. The drive home was just a short trip on the road to the next storm.

When the snow began to fall he went back to the same routine: check the house's battery lights, scan the yard for any loose debris, fill the tanks on the snowmobiles, and tip a little extra methanol in the gasoline.
